parole.testo: túl + nyomó, calque of German überwiegend.
From tükör (“mirror”) + tojás (“egg”), calque of German Spiegelei.
From German Türkis, from Old French pierre turqueise ("Turkish stone"), from turqueis (“Turkish”). The gem was named in the mistaken belief that it came from Turkestan.

parole.significato: cod (marine fish of the family Gadidae)
parole.testo: From tőke (“stump; stock”) + hal (“fish”). Calque of German Stockfisch. The first part in the German compound suggests that this fish was dried on a type of rod, perhaps a stake. First attested in 1604.
From German Universum, from Latin universus.

parole.significato: any toad in the family Bombinatoridae, i.e., toads of the genera Bombina and Barbourula, but especially fire-bellied to…
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from German Unke (“fire-bellied toad, Bombina sp.”).

parole.significato: urbanization, urbanisation (the process of the formation and growth of cities)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Urbanisation. With Latinate -áció ending.
From German urbanisieren. With -izál suffix.
Borrowed from German Uran.

parole.significato: train (the elongated back portion of a dress, such as a wedding gown or evening gown)
parole.testo: Contraction of the former collocation úszó alj (“the elongated back portion of a dress”). The nautical sense was shortened from uszály hajó (“barge boat”), a calque of German Schleppkahn (“barge”). First attested in 1822.

parole.significato: aftermath, aftereffect (any delayed effect; an effect which is not immediately manifested)
parole.testo: From utó- (“after-”) + hatás (“effect”), calque of German Nachwirkung. First attested in 1837.
From utó- (“post”) + irat (“writing”). Calque of German Nachschrift.
From utó- (“post-, after-”) + kor (“age”), calque of German Nachwelt. First attested in 1822.

parole.significato: afterword, epilogue (a brief oration or script at the end of a literary piece)
parole.testo: From utó- (“after-”) + szó (“word”), calque of German Nachwort. First attested in 1806.

parole.significato: aftertaste (the taste left in the mouth after consumption of food, drink, medicine, etc. that differs from its original…
parole.testo: From utó- (“after-”) + íz (“taste”), calque of German Nachgeschmack. First attested in 1836.

parole.significato: wild, romantic (so beautiful and majestic as something from a novel)
parole.testo: From vad (“wild”) + regényes (“romantic”), calque of German wildromantisch, from regény (“fiction, novel”) + -es (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: freight car, wagon (a railroad car drawn by a locomotive for carrying freight or, less frequently, people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Waggon.

parole.significato: tough, rough, ruffianly (ready to do things that are usually considered dangerous)
parole.testo: From the German Vagant, from the French vagant (“vagabond”), from vaguer (“to stray”), from the Latin vagārī (“to wander”), from vagus (“wandering”).

parole.significato: to mortar, plaster, render (to cover a wall with a layer of plaster)
parole.testo: First attested in 1588. Probably borrowed from German wacken, bewacken + -ol (verb-forming suffix), via Saxon stonemasons.

parole.significato: flash, camera flash (device used to produce a flash of artificial light)
parole.testo: Shortened from German Vakuumblitz, from Vakuum (“vacuum”) + Blitz (“camera flash”), from Latin vacuum (“void”).
Transliterated from German Walzer.
From German Walküre, from Old Norse valkyrja (“Valkyrie”, from valr (“the dead”) + kyrja (“chooser”)).
From való (“real”) + színű (“appearing”). Formed after German wahrscheinlich (“probable”) by translating the components, which takes its origin from Latin verisimilis (“probable”).
From the German argot Wamser (“thug, goon, tough”).
From German Vandalismus, from French vandalisme (“vandalism”), from Vandale (“Vandal”). With -izmus ending.
First attested in 1828. From vas (“iron”) + út (“way”), a calque of German Eisenbahn. Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries.
From German vegetativ. With -ív ending.

parole.significato: vegetarian (a person who does not eat any animal flesh)
parole.testo: From German Vegetarier, from Late Latin vegetarius.
Borrowed from German Wecker, more specifically from Austrian German.
From German Wende (“Wend, Sorbian”).

parole.significato: to ventilate (to let fresh air into a room or a building)
parole.testo: From German ventilieren, from Latin ventilo, from ventus (“wind”). With the verb-forming suffix -ál.
From German Ventilator. With -átor ending.
Borrowed from German Werbung (“recruitment”), from werben (“to recruit”).

parole.significato: verbunkos (an 18th-century Hungarian military genre of dance and music, typically divided into fast and slow sections)
parole.testo: From the archaic verbunk (“recruitment”, in turn from German Werbung (“recruitment”)) + -os (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: uppercase (set in majuscule or big letters, as opposed to the lowercase letters)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Versal (“capital letter”), from Medieval Latin versalis, from versus.

parole.significato: veteran (a person who has served in the armed forces, especially an old soldier who has seen long service)
parole.testo: From German Veteran, from Latin veteranus, from vetus (“old, aged, ancient”), veteris.
From German Witz (“joke”).
From German Vignette, from French vignette, diminutive of vigne (“vine”), from Latin vīnea, from vīnum (“wine”).
From German Wie geht’s?
From German Willi, from Slovak víly, plural of víla (“fairy”).

parole.significato: Weltschmerz, mal du siècle, world-weariness (apathetic or pessimistic view of life; depression concerning or discomfort…
parole.testo: From világ (“world”) + fájdalom (“pain”). Calque of German Weltschmerz.
From világ (“world”) + nézet (“view”), a calque of German Weltanschauung.

parole.significato: citizen of the world, global citizen, world citizen
parole.testo: From világ (“world”) + polgár (“citizen”). Possibly a calque of German Weltbürger.
From világ (“world”) + szemlélet (“point of view”), a calque of German Weltanschauung.
From German Vinyl, from Latin vinum.
From German Wirtschaft (“economy”), from Wirt (“host, landlord”).
Borrowed from German wirklich.
From German virtuell, from French virtuel. With -ális ending.
From German Virtuose, from Italian virtuoso.
From German virulent, from Latin virulentus. With -ens ending.

parole.significato: reflection (light reflected from a smooth surface, e.g. a mirror, the surface of water, etc.)
parole.testo: From vissz- (“back”) + fény (“light”). Calque of German Widerschein (“reflection”). Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries. First attested in 1815.

parole.significato: echo (a reflected sound that is heard again by its initial observer)
parole.testo: From vissz- (“back”) + hang (“sound”). Calque of German Widerhall (“echo”). The prefix is not attested as an independent word, it was shortened from vissza. Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries. First attested in 1777.

Lexicalization of viszontlátás (“the act of seeing again”) + -ra (“onto, to, for”, sublative case suffix), literally “until seeing each other again”, from viszontlát (“to see again”) + -ás (noun-forming suffix), from viszont- (“again, re-”) + lát (“to see”). From German visuell, from French visuel, from Latin visus (“sight”), from videre (“to see”). With -ális ending.
From German vokalisieren. With -izál suffix.
From German Wolfram.
From German Volant, from French volant.

parole.significato: train (line of connected cars or carriages)
parole.testo: From von (“to draw, pull”) + -at (noun-forming suffix). The currently common sense “train” is a semantic loan from German Zug (“pull, draught, train”); compare the development of English train.
From German Vulkan, from Latin Vulcanus (“Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and metalworking”).

parole.significato: fairground, amusement park, carnival (a row of show booths, businesses, and places of entertainment)
parole.testo: First attested in 1896. Borrowed from German Wurstelprater. Suffixed with -i to resolve the word-final consonant cluster, compare cetli from Bavarian zettl or German Zettel (/⁠ˈt͡sɛtl̩⁠/) etc.

parole.significato: slaughterhouse, shambles, abattoir (a place where animals are slaughtered)
parole.testo: From vágó (“slaughtering”) + híd (“bridge”), the latter because old slaughterhouses were usually built over a stream for easy cleaning. Calque of German Schlachtbrücke.
From German Vampir, from Serbo-Croatian vàmpīr (“vampire”).
From German wandern (“to wander”). With the verb-forming suffix -ol.
Borrowed from German Wangenkissen.

Calque of German Schutz-, based on the Hungarian verb véd (“to protect”) in present-participle sense (compare gyógy-, jár-, lát-). Some of its compounds were coined based on Hungarian compounds already coined.
véd- (“protecting, protective”) + jegy (“mark”), calque of German Schutzmarke.
From vér (“blood”) + szegény (“poor”). Calque of German blutarm. Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries. First attested in 1849.
vér (“blood”) + tanú (“witness”), calque of German Blutzeuge, itself influenced by Ancient Greek μάρτυς (mártus, “witness, martyr”)

parole.significato: making-of (a video featuring the behind the scenes of a show, film)
parole.testo: From German Werk (“work”) + film.

parole.significato: production still (photograph taken on the set of a movie during production)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Werkfoto, from Werk (“work”) + Foto (“photo”).
Borrowed from German Xenophobie.
From German Xylophon, from French xylophone, from Ancient Greek ξύλον (xúlon, “wood”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”).

parole.significato: jacket, suit coat (the upper piece of a suit or a short, elegant coat)
parole.testo: From the German Sakko (“coat”), from Sack, from the Italian sacco, from the English sack coat.
Internationalism via German Zebra. First attested in 1793.
Borrowed from German, from Latin sagum (“a military cloak”).

parole.significato: zenith (point in the sky vertically above a given position or observer; the point in the celestial sphere opposite the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Zenit, from Medieval Latin cenit, a transliteration of Arabic سَمْت (samt, “direction, path”) which is in itself a weak abbreviation of سَمْت الرَأْس (samt ar-raʔs, “direction of the head”).

parole.significato: chance, opportunity, slam dunk (a certain opportunity to achieve something, such as scoring in a sport or a business su…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Sitzer, from sitzen (“to sit”).
From German Jabot, from French jabot (“bird's crop”).
From German Gendarm (“gendarme”).

parole.significato: hinge (jointed or flexible device that allows the pivoting of a door, window, lid, or gate)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Scharnier.
From zseb (“pocket”) + kendő (“kerchief”). Possible calque of German Taschentuch.

parole.significato: genius (someone possessing extraordinary intelligence or skill)
parole.testo: From German Genie, from French génie, from Latin genius.
Borrowed from German Genialität, from French génialité (“geniality”). With Latinate -itás ending.
From German genial, from French génial (“genial”), from génie (“genius”). With -ális ending.
From German genant, from French gênant (“embarrassing”), present participle of gêner (“to bother, embarrass”).

parole.significato: shingle, tile (a small, thin piece of building material for laying in overlapping rows as a covering for the roof of a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German, more specifically from High German. Compare Middle High German schindel, Bavarian schintl, German Schindel.
Borrowed from German Sold, from Old French solt, from Late Latin soldum (“pay”), from Latin solidus (“golden coin”, literally “solid”).

parole.significato: plunder, loot (the goods attained via an act of plundering)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German, more specifically from High German. Compare Middle High German sachman (“robber”).

parole.significato: dead-end, blind alley, cul-de-sac, impasse (a street that leads nowhere)
parole.testo: From zsák (“sack”) + utca (“street”), calque of German Sackgasse (“dead-end”, literally “sack-street”), from Sack (“sack”) + Gasse (“street”).

parole.significato: genre, kind (stylistic category or sort, especially of literature or other artworks)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Genre.
From German Jour (“an at-home”), from French jour, from Vulgar Latin diurnum (“day”).

parole.significato: zone (area distinguished on the basis of a particular characteristic)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Zone, from Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “girdle, belt”).

parole.significato: to deal with a difficulty, to get on, to get one's act together
parole.testo: Literally, “to flounder onto [a] green branch”. It may be a calque of German auf (k)einen/den grünen Zweig kommen.
From Ádám (“Adam”) + kosztüm (“suit”), calque of German Adamskostüm.

parole.significato: agent (one who acts in place of another)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Agent, from French agent, from Latin agens (“agent”). With Latinate -ens ending.

parole.significato: coup d'état (sudden overthrow of a government by a small group of people)
parole.testo: From állam (“state”) + csíny (“coup”), calque of German Staatsstreich.
From állam (“state”) + polgár (“citizen”), calque of German Staatsbürger.

parole.significato: standpoint, point of view, viewpoint, view, outlook, position (an attitude, opinion, or set of beliefs)
parole.testo: From állás (“standing”) + pont (“point”), calque of German Standpunkt (“standpoint, point of view”). Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries. First attested in 1813.

parole.significato: amok (out of control, especially when armed and dangerous)
parole.testo: From ámok (“amok”) + futó (“runner”), partial calque of German Amokläufer, from Malay amuk (“to go on a killing spree”), from fut (“to run”) + -ó (present-participle suffix).

parole.significato: are (accepted SI unit of area equal to 100 square metres)
parole.testo: From German Ar (“are”) and French are (“are”), from Latin ārea (“threshing floor”).
From German As, from French as (“ace”), from Latin as (“a unit”).

From át (“across”, adverb) + -lag (an adverb-forming suffix thought to be noun-forming, also used in pamlag (“couch”)). Originally used as a technical term in geometry. The sense average is probably a calque of German Durchschnitt. First attested in 1839. Created during the Hungarian language reform

parole.significato: ebony (a hard, dense, deep black wood from various subtropical and tropical trees, especially of the genus Diospyros)
parole.testo: From German Eben(holz), from Latin ebenus, hebenus, from Ancient Greek ἕβενος (hébenos), ἔβενος (ébenos).
First attested in 1792. From ég + táj, a calque of German Himmelsgegend.

parole.significato: chamber pot, potty, jerry (container used for urination and defecation, particularly those used in early modern towns b…
parole.testo: From éjjeli (“night”) + edény (“pot”), calque of German Nachttopf.
From German Ära, from Late Latin aera, nominative plural of aes.
Borrowed from German Erz.

parole.significato: Estonian (of or relating to Estonia, its people or language)
parole.testo: From German Este (“Estonian”). Compare the etymology of English Estonia and ultimately Latin Aestiī.

parole.significato: vintage (wine identified by year and vineyard)
parole.testo: From év + járat, a calque of German Jahrgang.

parole.significato: Irish (of or relating to Ireland, its people or language)
parole.testo: From the German Ire (“Irishman”), from English Irish, from Old Irish Ériu (“Ireland”).
From German Oberst, from the superlative of ober (“the uppermost”). First attested in 1632.

parole.significato: to yammer (to cry or complain loudly)
parole.testo: From German oh weh + -gat (frequentative verb-forming suffix). First attested in 1708.

parole.significato: ocean (one of the large bodies of water separating the continents)
parole.testo: From German Ozean, from Latin Oceanus, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós, “the great earth-encircling river”).
Internationalism via German Ozon (“ozone”), from Ancient Greek ὄζον (ózon), neuter participle of ὄζω (ózō, “to smell”). First attested in 1846.
From German Ökologie, from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”). With -lógia ending.

parole.significato: econometrics (the branch of economics that applies statistical methods to the empirical study of economic theories and…
parole.testo: From German Ökonometrie.

parole.significato: economy (effective management of a community or system, or especially its resources)
parole.testo: From German Ökonomie.
From German Ökosystem.
From ököl (“fist”) + szabály (“rule”), possibly a calque of German Faustregel.

parole.significato: smug, self-important (having, or behaving as if having, too high of an opinion of one's own importance)
parole.testo: From ön- (“self”) + hitt (“believed”), from hisz (“to believe”) + -tt (past-participle suffix). Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries. Calque of German [Term?].

parole.significato: oenology (the scientific study of wines and winemaking)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Önologie, from scientific Latin oenologia, from Ancient Greek οἶνος (oînos, “wine”). With -lógia ending.
From ön- (“self”) + álló (“standing”). Calque of German selbstständig. Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries.
Borrowed from German Östrogen (“oestrogen”).

parole.significato: pathfinder, pathbreaker, trailblazer, pioneer (the first to establish a new path or approach)
parole.testo: From út (“path”) + törő (“breaker”). For the first sense: Calque of German Bahnbrecher. For the second sense: An approximate translation of the internationalism pionír.

parole.significato: Uzbek (of, or relating to Uzbekistan, its people or language)
parole.testo: From German Usbeke, from Ottoman Turkish اوزبك (özbek, “Uzbek”).
From űz + -em (noun-forming suffix). Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries. Calque of German Betrieb from betreiben and ultimately treiben.
űr (“space”) + hajó (“ship”), a calque of German Raumschiff.
An internationalism either via German Abstraktion (“abstraction”) or directly from Latin abstractiō (“separation; abstraction”), from abstrahō (“I draw away, drag away”). With -ció ending.

A Wanderwort, from a Romance language (e.g. French archiprêtre ← Old French archeprestre, Brescian Italian arsepret, Venetian Italian arsiprete) or from German Erzpriester; see more at English archpriest.

parole.significato: garland (a decorative wreath or cord, used at festive occasions)
parole.testo: Either via German Girlande or French guirlande, from Italian ghirlanda (“garland”).

parole.significato: gauze (a thin fabric with a loose, open weave used as a surgical dressing)
parole.testo: Either from German Gaze or French gaze, from Arabic قَزّ (qazz, “silk”).
From German ideal or from scientific Latin idealis. With -ális ending.
Either from a Slavic language, compare kelih, or from German Kelch.

First attested in 1811. Either from French mime (“pantomime actor”) or from German Mime, from Latin mimus (“mime actor”), from Ancient Greek μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”). With the verb-forming suffix -l. Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries.

parole.significato: palette (a thin board on which a painter lays and mixes colours)
parole.testo: Either from French palette or German Palette.

parole.significato: large-scale bribery, embezzlement or fraud, where an official provides an advantage to themselves or an associated pers…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Panama (“financial scandal, bribery”) or from German Panama-Skandal (“Panama scandals”).
From Viennese German Strizzi (“rogue, pimp”), of uncertain origin, either from Czech strýc (“uncle”) or Italian strizzare (“to wring, squeeze”).
Either from Italian tulipano or from Early New High German Tulipan (“tulip”), from Ottoman Turkish تولبند (tülbend), from Persian دلبند (dolband, “turban”)
